properties.decision:
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: "yes, promote this intent." Option (d) of the brainstorm; the roads not taken are kept below.

THE DECISION. A design's forward-looking schedule — which capabilities and requirements are expected at which epoch or increment — lives in the graph and is reached by QUESTION, not by document. His acceptance test, in his words: "what capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5" and "what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?" Nothing is written into git as an epoch snapshot: no epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. "Let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot" — rendering is an OUTPUT, produced on demand and thrown away, never the record.

WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, and it is narrower than the original idea: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, so "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" pins a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`). Forward-looking plans describe GRAPH content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe CODE and pin code. The information is in git either way, because the schedule lives in the graph and the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json` on every commit.

ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because they were genuinely considered.
(a) EPOCH BRANCHES — his own original mechanism, 2026-07-28: "epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1." A branch is the only place you can look at a future design whole, which is a real virtue. Not taken: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state and there is no future code to reflect; a full export is 1.6 MB, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON rewritten on every replan; branches invite merge semantics that do not apply; and a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` must be able to see.
(b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — my recommendation, and NOT TAKEN BECAUSE IT WAS WRONG rather than merely less good. Its selling point was that `git log -p` on the file would give the plan's revision history for free. But the schedule lives in the committed export, which already has git history and its own `prev_content_hash` chain — so the property existed and the file was an artifact added to obtain something the design already had. That is the shape this project keeps finding in other designs, found here in my own advice.
(c) RENDER TO FILES — the generated form of (b), carrying the same redundancy plus a staleness obligation.

THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT. Both of his questions are QUESTIONS, not documents: a query answers them directly, while a file answers them only if someone rendered the right one at the right moment. And every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves — `docs/design/reflow2.json` has a gate for it, `dataflow.html` has a check for it, and `docs/loop-model.json` demonstrated the failure the same day by becoming permanently unreproducible. Not materialising is the only way to have no drift at all.

MY EARLIER OBJECTION DID NOT HOLD, recorded because it was argued at length before being withdrawn: I claimed graph-only breaks readability for someone not running reflow2 (`req:design-reachable-without-the-repo`). It does not — the schedule is in the committed export, so it is reachable, merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.
properties.name: The schedule lives in the graph and is queried; nothing is snapshotted into git
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea, Anthony's lean, and Anthony's word to promote it. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` was reworded on the same word, because it described indexing git refs and that is no longer what it means; its original text is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`.

Worth keeping: the option that won is the one that ADDS NOTHING. No new file, no new branch, no new format, and — per the requirement it satisfies — largely no new storage, since epochs, Snapshots capturing incoming edges, and `compare_designs` already exist. The two rejected options both proposed materialising something, and both were arguing for a property the committed export already provides.

Also worth keeping, because it is a pattern rather than an incident: the file-per-epoch recommendation was mine, argued confidently, and wrong for the reason this project most often finds things wrong — it added a mechanism to obtain a property that already existed. Anthony's instinct to strip it back was better than my proposal to build it.
